meta.dataset: US federal treatment of receiving funds from China — the inbound side, which is where the real penalty exposure sits
meta.headline: The US does not tax a genuine gift or an inheritance received from China. What the US does impose is (a) information reporting with fixed and percentage penalties, and (b) income tax on income earned inside the Chinese account. The large penalties people actually experience are the information-return penalties in rows US-03 to US-05, not tax on the money.

rows.topic: Is a gift from a foreign individual taxable to the US recipient?
rows.value: No — a gift is not gross income. It must be reported on Form 3520 above the threshold, but no US tax is due on the gift itself.
rows.detail: IRC §6039F defines a reportable foreign gift as an amount the recipient treats as a gift or bequest. IRS guidance for gifts from foreign persons states the recipient completes Part IV of Form 3520 and notes the IRS may determine the income-tax consequences of the receipt where the form is late or wrong — i.e. reporting, not a gift tax on the recipient.
rows.implication: The frequently quoted 'you will pay 25% to bring the money in' is the §6039F(c) penalty for failing to file, not a tax on a gift. Filing removes it.
rows.source_title: Gifts from foreign person

rows.topic: Form 3520 filing threshold — gifts from a nonresident alien individual or foreign estate
rows.value: More than USD 100,000 in the aggregate for the tax year (related donors aggregated; not inflation-indexed)
rows.detail: IRS Instructions for Form 3520 (rev. 12/2025), Who Must File item 4: 1. More than $100,000 from a nonresident alien individual or a foreign estate (including foreign persons related to that nonresident alien individual or foreign estate) that you treated as gifts or bequests. IRS: if the gifts exceed $100,000 you must separately identify each gift in excess of $5,000.
rows.implication: A single transfer of USD 100,000 or less from a foreign individual triggers no Form 3520. Note the threshold applies to the aggregate for the year, and related donors (e.g. both parents) are combined.
rows.source_title: Instructions for Form 3520 (12/2025) — Who Must File; IRS 'Gifts from foreign person' page

rows.topic: Form 3520 filing threshold — gifts from a foreign corporation or partnership
rows.value: USD 20,116 for 2025; USD 20,573 for 2026 (inflation-adjusted)
rows.detail: IRS 'Gifts from foreign person': 对于来自外国公司或外国合伙企业的声称赠与…超过 $20,116 for 2025, and $20,573 for 2026 (adjusted annually for inflation).
rows.implication: A transfer framed as a 'gift from the family company' falls under a threshold one-fifth the size and requires the donor's identity to be disclosed. Framing matters.
rows.source_title: Gifts from foreign person — Reporting requirements

rows.topic: Penalty for a late or incomplete Form 3520 reporting a foreign gift
rows.value: 5% of the gift amount per month the failure continues, capped at 25% in aggregate
rows.detail: IRC §6039F(c)(1)(B): an amount equal to 5 percent of the amount of such foreign gift for each month for which the failure continues (not to exceed 25 percent of such amount in the aggregate). §6039F(c)(2): no penalty if the failure is due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect. IRS Instructions for Form 3520 restate this under 'Section 6039F'.
rows.implication: On a USD 500,000 gift, 25% is USD 125,000. This is almost certainly the 'considerable tax' the user has heard about. It is avoidable by filing; it is not a tax on the transfer.
rows.source_publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School — text of 26 U.S.C. §6039F
rows.source_title: 26 U.S. Code §6039F — Notice of large gifts received from foreign persons

rows.topic: FBAR — who must file and when
rows.value: US persons with a financial interest in, or signature authority over, foreign financial accounts whose aggregate value exceeded USD 10,000 at any time in the calendar year. Due 15 April, automatic extension to 15 October.
rows.detail: IRS FBAR page: 'a financial interest in or signature or other authority over at least one financial account located outside the United States if the aggregate value of those foreign financial accounts exceeded $10,000 at any time during the calendar year reported.' Filed on FinCEN Form 114, electronically, separately from the income tax return.
rows.implication: The Chinese bank account almost certainly triggers this already, whether or not any money is moved. This is the obligation most often missed and it has nothing to do with transferring funds.
rows.source_title: Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR)

rows.topic: FBAR civil penalty maximums
rows.value: Non-willful: up to USD 16,536 per violation. Willful: the greater of USD 165,353 or 50% of the account balance at the time of the violation.
rows.detail: 31 CFR 1010.821, Table 1, column 'penalties assessed on or after January 17, 2025': 31 U.S.C. 5321(a)(5)(B)(i) — Foreign Financial Agency Transaction, Non-Willful Violation of Transaction: statutory $10,000 → adjusted $16,536. 31 U.S.C. 5321(a)(5)(C)(i)(I) — Willful Violation of Transaction: statutory $100,000 → adjusted $165,353. The 50%-of-balance element is in 31 U.S.C. 5321(a)(5)(C).
rows.implication: Note the shape: the willful penalty is measured against the balance, so it scales with the size of the account rather than the size of any tax owed. This is the single largest downside in the whole problem, and it attaches to non-reporting, not to the transfer.
rows.source_publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register / FinCEN
rows.source_title: 31 CFR § 1010.821 — Penalty adjustment and table

rows.topic: Form 8938 (FATCA statement of specified foreign financial assets) — thresholds
rows.value: US-resident unmarried / MFS: > USD 50,000 at year end, or > USD 75,000 at any time. US-resident MFJ: > USD 100,000 / > USD 150,000. Living abroad, unmarried: > USD 200,000 / > USD 300,000. Living abroad, MFJ: > USD 400,000 / > USD 600,000.
rows.detail: IRS 'Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements'. Unlike the FBAR, Form 8938 is attached to the income tax return and is due with it, including extensions.
rows.implication: Form 8938 and the FBAR are separate obligations with different thresholds and different filing places. Filing one does not satisfy the other.
rows.source_title: Comparison of Form 8938 and FBAR requirements

rows.topic: Form 8938 penalty
rows.value: USD 10,000, plus up to USD 10,000 for each 30-day period after a 90-day notice, to a maximum additional USD 50,000
rows.detail: IRC §6038D(d)(1): a penalty of $10,000. §6038D(d)(2): if the failure continues more than 90 days after notice, an additional $10,000 for each 30-day period or fraction, capped at $50,000. §6038D(g): reasonable cause exception.
rows.implication: The 8938 penalty is a flat amount, so it is proportionally more painful on a small account than on a large one.
rows.source_publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School — text of 26 U.S.C. §6038D
rows.source_title: 26 U.S. Code §6038D — Information with respect to foreign financial assets

rows.topic: Section 988 — ordinary income treatment of foreign-currency gain
rows.value: Foreign-currency gain or loss on a §988 transaction is computed separately and treated as ordinary income or loss
rows.detail: IRC §988(a)(1)(A): any foreign currency gain or loss attributable to a section 988 transaction shall be computed separately and treated as ordinary income or loss. §988(e)(1)-(2): the section does not apply to an individual's personal transaction, and no gain is recognised on a personal transaction from exchange-rate movement — but that exclusion does not apply if the gain would exceed $200.
rows.implication: For an individual converting their own funds as a personal transaction, §988(e) means an FX gain of up to $200 is disregarded, but a larger gain is ordinary income. Note the mechanics: the gain is measured from the date the RMB was acquired at its USD cost, so a bank deposit held for years while the yuan moved can carry a real, reportable FX gain even though nothing was 'invested'.
rows.source_publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School — text of 26 U.S.C. §988
rows.source_title: 26 U.S. Code §988 — Treatment of certain foreign currency transactions

rows.topic: Which exchange rate a US filer must use
rows.value: The rate prevailing when the item is received, paid or accrued — for income items; the year-end rate for FBAR/8938 valuations of the account
rows.detail: IRS 'Foreign currency and currency exchange rates': if your functional currency is the US dollar you must immediately translate into dollars all items of income, expense, etc. that you receive, pay or accrue and that affect the computation of your income tax — using the exchange rate prevailing when you receive, pay or accrue the item. The FBAR comparison page separately states the FBAR uses the end-of-calendar-year rate, and Form 8938 the end-of-taxable-year rate.
rows.implication: Two different rates for two different purposes on the same account. Worth stating explicitly because it is a common error.
rows.source_title: Foreign currency and currency exchange rates

rows.topic: PFIC — what it is, for a US person holding a Chinese fund
rows.value: A foreign corporation is a PFIC if 75% or more of gross income is passive, or at least 50% of assets produce or are held to produce passive income
rows.detail: IRS Instructions for Form 8621 (12/2025), Definitions: income test 75%, asset test 50%. Form 8621 must be filed by a US person who is a direct or indirect shareholder of a PFIC in five listed circumstances.
rows.implication: A Chinese mutual fund, money-market fund or wealth-management product held by a US citizen is very likely a PFIC. This is the trap that turns a simple 'park it in a Chinese fund' idea into a punitive US tax outcome.
rows.source_title: Instructions for Form 8621 (12/2025)

rows.topic: §1291 excess-distribution regime — the punitive default
rows.value: Gain and excess distributions allocated across the whole holding period, taxed at the highest rate applicable in each year, plus an interest charge
rows.detail: IRC §1291(a)(1): the excess distribution is allocated ratably to each day in the holding period; only the current-year and pre-PFIC portions are included in income now; the tax is increased by the deferred tax amount under §1291(c). §1291(a)(2): on a disposition, all gain is treated as an excess distribution. IRS Instructions: the portions allocated to earlier PFIC years are not included in income but are subject to the separate tax and interest charge under §1291(c).
rows.implication: This is why PFIC exposure is described as the worst outcome in the US inbound system: the gain is pushed into past years at top marginal rates with compound interest, and there is no long-term capital-gain rate. A QEF or mark-to-market election (where available) changes the result, but both have their own conditions.
rows.source_publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School — text of 26 U.S.C. §1291
rows.source_title: 26 U.S. Code §1291 — Interest on tax deferral

rows.topic: Form 8621 $25,000 de minimis exception
rows.value: Part I need not be filed if the aggregate value of the shareholder's PFIC stock is USD 25,000 or less (USD 5,000 or less for indirect holdings)
rows.detail: IRS Instructions for Form 8621, Part I, Exceptions To Filing Part I: 'Exception if aggregate value of shareholder's PFIC stock is $25,000 or less' and 'Exception if the value of shareholder's indirect PFIC stock is $5,000 or less'.
rows.implication: A small holding may escape the annual information filing, but the §1291 tax regime itself still applies when the holding is disposed of. The filing exception is not a tax exception.
rows.source_title: Instructions for Form 8621 (12/2025) — Part I, Exceptions To Filing Part I

rows.topic: Section 4475 — 1% excise tax on cash-funded outbound remittance transfers
rows.value: 1% of the transfer amount; applies to transfers made after 31 December 2025; only where the sender funds with cash, a money order, a cashier's check, traveller's check or similar physical instrument. Funds drawn from a financial-institution account, or paid by a US-issued debit or credit card, are outside the tax.
rows.detail: IRC §4475, added by Pub. L. 119-21 §70604(a) (4 July 2025). §4475(a) imposes 1%; §4475(b)(1) the sender pays; §4475(b)(2) the provider collects and remits quarterly; §4475(c) limits it to cash and similar physical instruments; §4475(d) excludes account withdrawals and US-issued cards. Effective for transfers after 31 December 2025 (§70604(c)). IRS Notice 2025-55 gives failure-to-deposit relief for the first three quarters of 2026. Proposed regulations REG-114499-25 (April 2026) are not final.
rows.implication: This runs the other direction (US to abroad), so it does not tax the user's inbound transfer. It matters for the reverse leg if they later send money to China, and it is a live example of how a 'penalty on moving money' story starts: a 1% excise tax that does not apply if you use a bank transfer instead of cash.
rows.source_publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School — text of 26 U.S.C. §4475
rows.source_title: 26 U.S. Code §4475 — Imposition of tax (remittance transfers)
rows.verification_note: Statute text and effective date verified from the U.S. Code. IRS Notice 2025-55 and the proposed regulations were seen in search results but the Notice PDF was not opened directly; the relief description should be re-checked before being relied on.

rows.topic: Carrying or shipping currency into the US
rows.value: More than USD 10,000 at one time must be reported to CBP on FinCEN Form 105. There is no limit on the amount.
rows.detail: CBP 'Money and Other Monetary Instruments': federal law mandates that when entering or leaving the United States you must report amounts exceeding $10,000 to CBP; the threshold applies to the total a family or group is carrying collectively, not per individual; filing is available electronically at fincen105.cbp.dhs.gov. Monetary instruments include US or foreign coins and currency, traveller's checks, and negotiable instruments in bearer or transferable form.
rows.implication: Cash is a lawful but operationally hopeless route for a large sum: 3% of a USD 1m balance is USD 30,000 per trip, and repeated small trips invite a structuring analysis.
rows.source_title: Money and Other Monetary Instruments

rows.topic: Delinquent FBAR / information-return remediation
rows.value: Streamlined Filing Compliance Procedures: available to individuals certifying non-willful conduct, with a reduced or no offshore penalty depending on residence
rows.detail: IRS Streamlined Filing Compliance Procedures: available to US individual taxpayers residing inside and outside the US; the taxpayer must certify that the failure to report all income, pay all tax and submit all information returns (including FBARs) was due to non-willful conduct, defined as negligence, inadvertence, mistake, or a good-faith misunderstanding of the law. Not available if the IRS has already begun a civil examination or a criminal investigation. Two tracks: Streamlined Foreign Offshore Procedures and Streamlined Domestic Offshore Procedures.
rows.implication: This is the concrete answer to 'how do I fix a non-compliance problem rather than pay the maximum penalty'. Which track applies depends on non-residency, and the domestic track carries a miscellaneous offshore penalty that the IRS page describes on the sub-page.
rows.source_title: Streamlined filing compliance procedures

rows.topic: Gifts the US person makes — who pays US gift tax
rows.value: The US donor, not the foreign recipient. Annual exclusion USD 19,000 per recipient for 2026; basic exclusion amount USD 15,000,000 for 2026.
rows.detail: IRS IR-2025-103 / Rev. Proc. 2025-32: for tax year 2026 the annual exclusion for gifts remains $19,000, and estates of decedents dying during 2026 have a basic exclusion amount of $15,000,000 (up from $13,990,000 for 2025).
rows.implication: Relevant to the reverse direction (giving money away), and to the annual exclusion for gifts to a non-citizen spouse, which rises to USD 194,000 for 2026. Not a tax on receiving.
rows.source_title: IRS releases tax inflation adjustments for tax year 2026 (IR-2025-103; Rev. Proc. 2025-32)

rows.topic: Is there a US–China income tax treaty that helps here?
rows.value: A treaty exists (1984, with protocol), but it does not convert a capital-account transfer into a current-account one, and most treaties contain a saving clause preserving US taxation of citizens
rows.detail: IRS 'United States income tax treaties - A to Z' lists China and states that most treaties contain a saving clause which prevents a citizen or resident of the United States from using a treaty provision to avoid taxation of US-source income.
rows.implication: A treaty is not a route around the FX rules — exchange control is unilateral domestic law. The treaty's relevance is limited to double-tax relief and reduced withholding, and the saving clause limits even that for a US citizen.
rows.source_title: United States income tax treaties — A to Z

rows.topic: FATCA / information exchange with China — the enforcement backdrop
rows.value: China is listed by Treasury as a Model 1 jurisdiction treated as having an IGA in effect 'in substance'; no signed agreement was located
rows.detail: Treasury's FATCA jurisdiction list classifies China as 'Agreement in Substance' / Model 1. A 2016 Congressional Research Service report reproduces the same classification. The signed China IGA text itself was not retrieved, and no Chinese domestic implementing rules were retrieved either.
rows.implication: FLAGGED. The practical implication — that a US person's Chinese account is not invisible — is a reasonable reading of the Treasury listing, but the operative legal instruments were not verified. Do not treat this row as proof of automatic bank-account reporting from China.
rows.source_title: FATCA Reporting on U.S. Accounts: Recent Legal Developments — jurisdiction table

rows.topic: Streamlined domestic offshore procedures — the offshore penalty for a US resident
rows.value: 5% of the highest aggregate balance/value of the unreported foreign assets over the covered period
rows.detail: IRS 'U.S. taxpayers residing in the United States': the Title 26 miscellaneous offshore penalty is equal to 5 percent of the highest aggregate balance/value of the taxpayer's foreign financial assets that are subject to the penalty during the years in the covered tax return period and the covered FBAR period. Eligible filers must submit amended returns for the most recent 3 years, delinquent FBARs for the most recent 6 years, and pay the penalty; in exchange they are subject only to that penalty and not to accuracy-related, information-return or FBAR penalties. Requires a previously filed return for each of the 3 most recent years.
rows.implication: This is the concrete quantitative answer to 'how much does it cost to fix a missed filing rather than be caught'. Compare with the willful FBAR maximum of 50% of the balance (US-06).
rows.source_title: U.S. taxpayers residing in the United States — Streamlined domestic offshore procedures

rows.topic: Streamlined foreign offshore procedures — no offshore penalty
rows.value: 0% miscellaneous offshore penalty, provided the non-residency requirement is met
rows.detail: IRS 'U.S. taxpayers residing outside the United States': eligible filers file delinquent or amended returns for the most recent 3 years plus delinquent FBARs for the most recent 6 years and remit the tax and interest; they 'will not be subject to failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties, accuracy-related penalties, information return penalties, or FBAR penalties'. Non-residency for a US citizen requires, in at least one of the most recent three years, no US abode and physical presence outside the US for at least 330 full days.
rows.implication: This is the single most valuable fact in the whole dataset: for a US citizen who has genuinely been living outside the US, the entire penalty exposure can be eliminated by filing under this procedure and paying only the tax and interest that was actually due. It is the difference between 0% and 50% of the account balance.
rows.source_title: U.S. taxpayers residing outside the United States — Streamlined Foreign Offshore Procedures
